name: Bromelain

lead: Bromelain is a mix of protein-digesting enzymes from pineapple stem. People take it to cut down swelling and bruising after cosmetic surgery or injury, and some use it for general puffiness and inflammation.

Its enzyme activity is thought to modulate inflammatory mediators such as bradykinin and prostaglandins and affect fibrin breakdown. Systematic reviews cover post-surgical swelling and pain, osteoarthritis and other inflammatory conditions, with small, mixed trials. A topical form is approved in Europe for removing dead tissue from burns.

paras: Taken as capsules or tablets, often started before and continued after a procedure, or used with other recovery supplements such as arnica. Some also use it as a digestive enzyme. Potency varies between products.

Side effects include stomach upset and allergic reactions, especially in people allergic to pineapple. It may increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants and can interact with some antibiotics. Supplement potency is inconsistent. Legal as a supplement.

web.title: Arnica and bromelain after facial surgery (clinic guide)

angle.text: Bromelain is taken to reduce swelling and bruising, notably after surgery or injury, so puffiness fades and healing looks faster. Studies have examined post-surgical swelling with mixed results; everyday facial puffiness use is anecdotal.

lead: Bromelain is an extract from pineapple, mainly the stem, containing a mixture of protein-digesting (proteolytic) enzymes and smaller amounts of other compounds.[1] The best-known enzymes are stem bromelain and fruit bromelain, both sulfhydryl (cysteine) proteases.[1] It is used industrially as a meat tenderiser and in baking and cosmetics manufacturing, and is sold as an oral supplement aimed at swelling, bruising and general inflammation.[1][2]

For appearance, the main draw is recovery. Patients and surgeons discuss bromelain, often paired with arnica, as an option for reducing visible swelling and bruising after rhinoplasty, jaw surgery and other facial procedures, so that the face looks like itself sooner.[3][4][5][6] In training circles it is used for sore joints and tendons and as a digestive enzyme, which people link to training more consistently and eating enough to build size.[7][8][9]

The one regulator-approved medical use is topical. NexoBrid, a bromelain-enriched enzyme concentrate, was authorised across the EU on 18 December 2012 to remove burn eschar.[10] For oral supplements, published work includes systematic reviews, trials after dental, periodontal and breast surgery, and in vitro and animal pharmacology, with heterogeneous and often small studies.[11][12][13][14][15]
infobox: Post-procedure swelling and bruising; training recovery
Sold as a dietary supplement in many countries

paras: Commercial bromelain is an extract rather than a single molecule. It is a mixture of sulfhydryl proteases plus minor components, and the term has been applied both to the individual enzymes and to the whole extract [1]. It is produced mostly in pineapple-growing countries such as Thailand and Malaysia from stems, peel, leaves or processing waste, which are blended, filtered, purified and concentrated [1].

The stem is the most common commercial source because usable quantities can be extracted after the fruit is harvested.[1] The enzymes are heat labile: cooked or canned pineapple does not tenderise meat, and the amount in an ordinary serving of fruit is probably small compared with extracted supplements.[1] Wikipedia reports that stem bromelain retains most of its activity at body temperature and that concentrated solutions keep activity for at least a week at room temperature.[1] Because composition and enzyme activity vary between products, reviews note that potency is not uniform across supplements.[2]

Pineapple has a long tradition of medicinal use among peoples of South and Central America.[1][12] Bromelain was first isolated in 1891 by the Venezuelan chemist Vicente Marcano through fermenting pineapple fruit. In 1892 Russell Chittenden, Elliott Joslin and Frank Meara studied it more fully and named it bromelin; the term bromelain was later applied to proteases from any plant of the family Bromeliaceae.[1]

A 1969 controlled clinical report in a plastic-surgery journal described bromelain as a proteolytic enzyme in the context of tissue swelling, an early link between the extract and surgical recovery.[16] A dermatology news column describes a 1962 randomised study of 53 rhinoplasty patients reporting that swelling and bruising lasted about 2 days with bromelain versus 7 days with placebo, and a later randomised study of 154 facial plastic surgery patients that found no significant difference in swelling compared with placebo.[17] A 2006 review in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery summarised its use in that field.[18]

Bromelain-enriched enzymes were later developed as a topical burn product, with the European Medicines Agency's committee adopting its opinion on NexoBrid on 20 September 2012 and the EU authorisation following on 18 December 2012; the holder is MediWound Germany.[10]

Bromelain is used in three broad ways: as an oral supplement for swelling and inflammation, as an ingredient in combination bruising products, and, in a distinct pharmaceutical form, as a topical debriding agent for burns.

Bromelain is promoted for reducing swelling and bruising after facial and body procedures, and is sometimes combined with arnica.[3][4][6] A Sydney plastic surgery practice's patient guide says patients may use arnica and bromelain after discussing it with their surgeon, describes them as an optional extra beside technique and aftercare, and says the evidence is limited and mixed.[6] The same guide advises that bromelain is stopped two weeks before surgery and not combined with blood thinners, and that if used afterwards it starts 48 hours after the operation.[6]

A registered trial is evaluating bromelain for facial swelling after jaw surgery, and a trial of arnica with bromelain after rhinoplasty was registered but withdrawn.[3][4] The guide also cites a 2025 rhinoplasty trial of 46 patients that reported less bruising and bleeding at day 7 with no difference in swelling.[6] An over-the-counter bruising supplement listed on DailyMed combines bromelain with arnica, vitamin C, zinc and bioflavonoids, describing itself as nutritional support during recovery.[5]

The established medical product is topical: a bromelain-enriched enzyme concentrate for removing dead tissue from deep partial- and full-thickness burns.[1][10] Oral bromelain has been studied for osteoarthritis, sinusitis, post-operative swelling in dental and plastic surgery, ulcerative colitis, and as an adjunct in oncology and infection research.[11][19][14][20] Memorial Sloan Kettering's herb summary lists anti-inflammatory activity, arthritis, burns and swelling among the claimed uses.[21]

Reviews describe antioedematous, anti-inflammatory, antithrombotic and fibrinolytic activities of bromelain in vitro and in animals, and propose that these depend in part on proteolytic activity, with the active factors only partly characterised [2]. A 2025 systematic review of in vitro studies found that bromelain reduced secretion of the cytokines IL-1 beta, IL-6 and TNF-alpha from stimulated immune cells [13]. Proposed effects on bradykinin, prostaglandins and fibrin breakdown appear in reviews of its pharmacology [2][19].
The Sloan Kettering page notes that anti-clotting effects appear in laboratory studies, while no clinical trial has shown treatment of circulatory disorders.[21]

A 2023 systematic review reported that bromelain can be detected in serum with retained proteolytic activity after oral intake, but how much reaches tissues and whether this explains clinical effects remains discussed in the literature [11][2].

The European Medicines Agency describes NexoBrid as a concentrate of proteolytic enzymes enriched in bromelain, extracted from pineapple plant stems, which dissolve burn eschar so that underlying tissue can heal. It is prescription-only, applied by trained staff in specialised burn centres, and left on the skin for four hours.[10]

In a study of 156 patients, about 15% of NexoBrid-treated wounds needed surgical eschar removal versus about 63% with standard debridement, and in a study of 145 patients from birth to 18 years, complete eschar removal took about one day on average versus about six days with standard care. Fever and pain are the most common side effects, and the product must not be used in people allergic to pineapple, papaya or papain.[10] This burn product is a separate pharmaceutical use from oral supplements.

A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis covering 54 articles, 39 of which were meta-analysed, assessed efficacy and safety of bromelain across conditions and reported heterogeneity among studies [11]. A 2024 systematic review in Nutrients and a 2021 review summarised possible applications in cardiovascular, inflammatory, infectious and oncological contexts while stating that further mechanistic and clinical work is needed [12][19].

Surgical settings have received the most attention. A double-blind randomised trial of 114 breast-conserving surgery patients tested a supplement containing bromelain with Boswellia phytosome, with or without alpha-lipoic acid, superoxide dismutase, vitamins and centella, versus placebo for 30 days; the combination arm showed less oedema than placebo, so the effect cannot be attributed to bromelain alone [15]. Other trials examined oral bromelain after periodontal surgery and third-molar extraction [14][22], and an ulcerative colitis trial and a dental plaque enzyme pre-rinse trial have been published [20][23].

Registered trials include studies on facial swelling after jaw surgery, third-molar surgery, diabetic foot ulcers, root-canal medication, cough, and intratumoral use in pseudomyxoma peritonei [3][24][25][26][27][28]. No large randomised trial of oral bromelain for cosmetic-procedure bruising in healthy people appears among the published studies reviewed.

Memorial Sloan Kettering's summary states that small clinical studies suggest reduced pain, swelling and bleeding after procedures such as third-molar and periodontal surgery, and describes the evidence in arthritis as mixed, with some small studies showing knee-pain benefit and others not.[21]

Reviews describe bromelain as having low toxicity and few side effects [2][19]. A DailyMed label for a bromelain-containing bruising supplement lists mild gastrointestinal discomfort, nausea and skin rash, rare hypersensitivity reactions and prolonged bleeding as possible reactions, and advises caution with anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs and stopping use two weeks before surgery [5].

Sloan Kettering's summary lists allergic reactions including contact cheilitis, IgE-mediated allergy and fixed drug eruption, and notes preclinical data suggesting increased bruising and bleeding risk with warfarin (clinical relevance undetermined), possible increases in tetracycline levels, and in vitro CYP2C9 inhibition of unknown significance.[21] A dermatology column lists children, people allergic to pineapple or bee stings, people with heart palpitations and those on blood thinners as contraindicated.[17] The page recommends patients tell their surgical team about any supplements they take.[21]

A DailyMed label for a bromelain-containing bruising product advises stopping use two weeks before surgery.[5] One T Nation user on dual antiplatelet therapy after stent placement reported spontaneous gum bleeding when adding bromelain, which he took as a warning sign.[29]

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and training communities
paras: On T Nation, bromelain appears in individual supplement lists alongside fish oil, collagen, glucosamine and CoQ10,[7][30] in discussions of tendon and elbow pain management,[9] and as a digestive-enzyme suggestion during bulking.[8] A poster recalled that retail supplement shops sold it for anti-inflammatory purposes and asked whether pineapple juice was used for the same reason.[31] Another forum user suggested a daily bromelain and NAC regimen in a COVID-19 thread.[32] Discussion is largely anecdotal.

Arnica is the supplement most often named alongside bromelain in facial-surgery recovery. Trials of arnica after rhinoplasty and eyelid surgery have reported mixed results, and the Sydney guide says a 2026 review of facial surgery found arnica may reduce bruising and swelling while evidence for bromelain is more limited.[6] The author of a clinician news column describes faster bruising resolution after cosmetic procedures from clinical experience while stating that no formal study was done.[17]
Bromelain is sold as a dietary supplement; the regulatory approval cited by Wikipedia and the EMA is the European authorisation of the topical burn debridement product.[1][10]
Bromelain is often discussed alongside other swelling and recovery supports such as arnica, boswellia, collagen and papain, a related plant protease that is also used as a meat tenderiser.[1][7][6]

lore.intro: In training and recovery forums bromelain is described as a pineapple-derived anti-inflammatory and enzyme supplement, mentioned in stacks for joints, bruising and digestion [9][7][8].

Eating pineapple provides the same benefits as the supplement
It acts as a digestive enzyme that helps with large food intake
Bromelain can thin the blood and cause bleeding with antiplatelet drugs

Bromelain is a natural alternative to anti-inflammatory drugs
